Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On April 7, 2022, the Surface Transportation Board (STB) announced it would hold a public hearing on April 26 and 27, 2022, to address urgent and widespread rail service issues. [2] The board noted it had received reports from the Secretary of Agriculture and other stakeholders about the serious impact of unreliable service on rail users, particularly shippers of agricultural and energy products. [2] At the hearing, more than 25 rail-shipper groups and all rail-worker unions provided testimony. [3] U.S. Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg, the first to hold that office to testify before the STB in over 20 years, stated that the agriculture industry was being "significantly impacted by the railroad's service delays, especially when it comes to obtaining the necessary amount of fertilizer and chemicals that are critical for the growing season." [3] Deputy Secretary of Agriculture Jewel Bronaugh also testified, noting that shippers in the Midwest had grain they were unable to ship, causing elevators to fill up and preventing them from purchasing more grain from farmers, while livestock operations could not receive necessary grain for feed. [5] Testimony from Landus Coop in Iowa stated they could only load half their shipments and had to turn away farmers, consistent with the broader issues addressed at the hearing.

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On April 7, 2022, the Surface Transportation Board (STB) announced it would hold a public hearing on April 26 and 27, 2022, to address urgent and widespread rail service issues. [2] The board noted it had received reports from the Secretary of Agriculture and other stakeholders about the serious impact of unreliable service on rail users, particularly shippers of agricultural and energy products. [2] At the hearing, more than 25 rail-shipper groups and all rail-worker unions provided testimony. [3] U.S. Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg, the first to hold that office to testify before the STB in over 20 years, stated that the agriculture industry was being "significantly impacted by the railroad's service delays, especially when it comes to obtaining the necessary amount of fertilizer and chemicals that are critical for the growing season." [3] Deputy Secretary of Agriculture Jewel Bronaugh also testified, noting that shippers in the Midwest had grain they were unable to ship, causing elevators to fill up and preventing them from purchasing more grain from farmers, while livestock operations could not receive necessary grain for feed. [5] Testimony from Landus Coop in Iowa stated they could only load half their shipments and had to turn away farmers, consistent with the broader issues addressed at the hearing. <2> The National Corn Growers Association (NCGA), along with 25 of its state affiliates, issued a letter to U.S. trade and agriculture officials warning that fertilizer prices were approaching 'disastrous levels.' The NCGA stated that the combination of low corn prices, trade uncertainty, and persistently high input costs—made worse by countervailing duties and tariffs—had created a 'calamitous environment' for farmers planning for harvest and the subsequent planting season. The organization highlighted that fertilizer can represent over 30 percent of a row crop farmer's input costs and that the tariff war was exacerbating already high prices.

[1] He estimated that global grain prices could increase by a range of 10 to 15%. [5] The drought expanded, with 58% of the region classified as being in moderate drought or worse. [4, 5] These dry conditions affected 64% of the U.S. corn production area and 57% of the soybean production area. [4, 5] The widespread dryness fueled significant concerns over potential harvest shortfalls, causing corn and soybean prices to surge to multi-month highs. [2] This price disparity, combined with larger projected corn supplies from Brazil, was expected to diminish prospects for U.S. exports for the remainder of the 2022/23 marketing year. [1] The forecast also included optimistic demand, with anticipated increases in corn usage for livestock feed, ethanol production, and exports. [1] Consequently, the USDA projected a significant drop in the national average farm price for corn to $4.80 per bushel for the 2023-24 marketing year, a substantial decrease from the estimated $6.60 per bushel for the 2022-23 marketing year. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> ...a significant improvement in market fundamentals for corn and soybeans...; ...over the three months leading up to February.; ...and a surprising drop in the U.S. corn yield estimate in the January WASDE report... <2> The University of Georgia projected an agriculture outlook for 2025.; The outlook cited a strong U.S. dollar as a contributing factor to economic outcomes.; The outlook cited trade policy uncertainty as a contributing factor to economic outcomes. <3> The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) Commitments of Traders report for the week ending December 10, 2024, showed that 'Managed Money' funds held a significant net long position in corn futures and options. The data, published on Friday, December 13, 2024, provides a breakdown of open interest for futures and options markets. The positioning by these speculative traders, often anticipating future price movements, is a key indicator for market trends. The CFTC releases these reports weekly, with data collected as of Tuesday and typically published on Friday. <4> In its World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates (WASDE) report released on December 10, 2024, the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) increased its forecast for corn used for ethanol in the 2024-25 marketing year. The projection was raised by 50 million bushels to 5.5 billion bushels, up from the previous month's forecast of 5.45 billion. The season-average corn price received by producers was projected to remain unchanged at $4.10 per bushel. <5> The USDA's weekly export sales report for the week ending October 17, 2024, showed corn sales totaling a significant 4.18 million metric tons (164.7 million bushels). This sales volume is among the highest in the last two decades, surpassed by only four other weeks, all of which occurred in early 2021. Notably, this peak was reached without substantial purchases from China, which bought only 10,000 tons. The strong sales figures reflect robust global demand for U.S. corn, bolstered by plentiful domestic supplies and globally competitive pricing. <6> On Monday, October 21, 2024, December corn futures experienced a notable increase, closing the day at $4.09 ½, which was up by 4¾ cents. This upward trend was largely driven by strong export demand, highlighted by several flash sales announced by the USDA for the 2024/2025 marketing year. The specific sales included 169,926 metric tons of corn to Mexico, 130,000 metric tons to South Korea, and 198,192 metric tons to undisclosed destinations. <7> The USDA's World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates (WASDE) report for October, released on October 11, 2024, resulted in a 2-cent decrease in corn prices immediately following its publication. [1] For the 2024/2025 marketing year, the report indicated an increase in U.S. corn production estimates by 17 million bushels, bringing the total forecast to 15.2 billion bushels. [2, 3, 7] Concurrently, the national average corn yield forecast was raised by 0.2 bushels per acre, from a previous estimate to a record 183.8 bushels per acre. [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] Despite the increased production forecast, the report also noted smaller overall supplies due to lower beginning stocks, leading to a reduction in projected ending stocks by 58 million bushels to 2.0 billion. [2, 7] <8> The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) reported that for the week ending October 4, 2024, domestic fuel ethanol production increased by over 3% to an average of 1.038 million barrels per day. This was an increase of 23,000 barrels per day from the previous week's average of 1.015 million barrels per day. In addition to the production rise, ethanol stocks decreased significantly by nearly 6%, falling to 22.154 million barrels from 23.549 million the week prior. The data, which also noted a 38% increase in exports, indicates strong demand within the ethanol sector, a key consumer of U.S. corn. <9> Based on the USDA's National Agricultural Statistics Service weekly report, 21% of the U.S. corn harvest was complete as of September 29, 2024. [2] This represents a 7-percentage-point increase from the prior week. [2] The harvest pace was equal to the previous year and 3 percentage points ahead of the five-year average of 18%. [2, 1] Favorable warm and dry weather conditions in key growing areas contributed to the accelerated progress by aiding the dry-down and harvesting process. [2] The report also noted that 75% of the corn crop had reached maturity, which is 5 points ahead of the five-year average. [2, 1]

The data, published on Friday, December 13, 2024, provides a breakdown of open interest for futures and options markets. The positioning by these speculative traders, often anticipating future price movements, is a key indicator for market trends. The CFTC releases these reports weekly, with data collected as of Tuesday and typically published on Friday. <4> In its World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates (WASDE) report released on December 10, 2024, the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) increased its forecast for corn used for ethanol in the 2024-25 marketing year. The projection was raised by 50 million bushels to 5.5 billion bushels, up from the previous month's forecast of 5.45 billion. The season-average corn price received by producers was projected to remain unchanged at $4.10 per bushel. <5> The USDA's weekly export sales report for the week ending October 17, 2024, showed corn sales totaling a significant 4.18 million metric tons (164.7 million bushels). This sales volume is among the highest in the last two decades, surpassed by only four other weeks, all of which occurred in early 2021. Notably, this peak was reached without substantial purchases from China, which bought only 10,000 tons. The strong sales figures reflect robust global demand for U.S. corn, bolstered by plentiful domestic supplies and globally competitive pricing. <6> On Monday, October 21, 2024, December corn futures experienced a notable increase, closing the day at $4.09 ½, which was up by 4¾ cents. This upward trend was largely driven by strong export demand, highlighted by several flash sales announced by the USDA for the 2024/2025 marketing year. The specific sales included 169,926 metric tons of corn to Mexico, 130,000 metric tons to South Korea, and 198,192 metric tons to undisclosed destinations. <7> The USDA's World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates (WASDE) report for October, released on October 11, 2024, resulted in a 2-cent decrease in corn prices immediately following its publication. [1] For the 2024/2025 marketing year, the report indicated an increase in U.S. corn production estimates by 17 million bushels, bringing the total forecast to 15.2 billion bushels. [2, 3, 7] Concurrently, the national average corn yield forecast was raised by 0.2 bushels per acre, from a previous estimate to a record 183.8 bushels per acre. [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] Despite the increased production forecast, the report also noted smaller overall supplies due to lower beginning stocks, leading to a reduction in projected ending stocks by 58 million bushels to 2.0 billion. [2, 7] <8> The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) reported that for the week ending October 4, 2024, domestic fuel ethanol production increased by over 3% to an average of 1.038 million barrels per day. This was an increase of 23,000 barrels per day from the previous week's average of 1.015 million barrels per day. In addition to the production rise, ethanol stocks decreased significantly by nearly 6%, falling to 22.154 million barrels from 23.549 million the week prior. The data, which also noted a 38% increase in exports, indicates strong demand within the ethanol sector, a key consumer of U.S. corn. <9> Based on the USDA's National Agricultural Statistics Service weekly report, 21% of the U.S. corn harvest was complete as of September 29, 2024. [2] This represents a 7-percentage-point increase from the prior week. [2] The harvest pace was equal to the previous year and 3 percentage points ahead of the five-year average of 18%. [2, 1] Favorable warm and dry weather conditions in key growing areas contributed to the accelerated progress by aiding the dry-down and harvesting process. [2] The report also noted that 75% of the corn crop had reached maturity, which is 5 points ahead of the five-year average. [2, 1]

The report indicated that the average price received by U.S. farmers for corn in November 2025 was $3.98 per bushel, an increase of 5 cents from October but a decrease of 9 cents compared to November 2024. <2> On December 31, 2025, the USDA announced commodity-specific national payment rates for the Farmer Bridge Assistance (FBA) Program, which is part of a broader $12 billion economic relief package for farmers. The FBA Program utilizes $11 billion to deliver one-time bridge payments to U.S. row crop farmers to help offset projected 2025 losses and provide cash flow heading into the 2026 planting season. The relief aims to mitigate the impacts of depressed commodity prices, temporary trade market disruptions, and elevated input costs. The final per-acre payment rates include a flat rate of $44.36 for corn, $132.89 for rice, $117.35 for cotton, $81.75 for oats, $55.65 for peanuts, $48.11 for sorghum, $39.35 for wheat, $30.88 for soybeans, and $20.51 for barley. <3> In its December World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates (WASDE) report, the USDA increased its 2025-26 U.S. corn export expectations by 125 million bushels to a total of 3.2 billion bushels. Because all other demand categories remained unchanged, this upward revision directly lowered projected ending stocks by the same amount, bringing them down to 2.029 billion bushels. Despite these supply and demand adjustments, the projected season-average farm price for corn was maintained at $4.00 per bushel. <4> The USDA released its November WASDE report, slightly lowering the U.S. corn yield estimate to 186 bushels per acre and adjusting total production to 16.75 billion bushels. The report also raised corn export forecasts to a record 3.075 billion bushels and increased ending stocks to 2.154 billion bushels. <5> A 43-day U.S. federal government shutdown, which began on October 1, 2025, and concluded on November 12, 2025, resulted in a severe blackout of critical agricultural and market data. During the peak harvest season, the lapse in funding halted the publication of vital reports, including USDA NASS crop progress updates, WASDE, export sales numbers, and CFTC Commitments of Traders (COT) reports. This data blackout left farmers and traders operating blindly, resulting in increased uncertainty, heightened market volatility, and a greater reliance on alternative market signals like satellite imagery. Following the signing of a funding bill on November 12, government operations and official reporting resumed, with the CFTC planning to clear its chronological report backlog by December 29, 2025. <6> A survey conducted between October 13-17, 2025, revealed a significant divergence in farmer sentiment, described as a 'tale of two economies.' Livestock producers expressed strong optimism, partly driven by record-high profitability in the beef sector. In contrast, crop producers reported a notably more pessimistic outlook due to poor profit margins across major crop enterprises. In response to low corn prices, the survey specifically asked corn producers about their plans for the 2026 season. The results showed that 29% intended to reduce phosphorus applications, and 27% planned to adopt lower-cost seed traits or varieties. Meanwhile, 30% of the surveyed corn producers did not anticipate making any changes to their production practices. The findings of this survey were published on November 4, 2025. <7> Wyffels Hybrids, a seed company, announced on November 4, 2025, that as of October 29, 2025, the average yield from its 724 harvested test plots was 241 bushels per acre (bpa). This represented a decrease from the 247 bpa final average recorded across 841 sites in 2024. The data indicated lower year-over-year yields in its Illinois and Iowa plots; Illinois was down 8 bushels to 252 bpa, and Iowa's average dropped by 21 bushels to 228 bpa. The company attributed the decline primarily to disease pressures, with tar spot being the main factor north of Interstate 80 and southern rust being more prominent farther south. <8> Following a meeting on October 31, 2025, the U.S. and China reached a significant trade and economic deal to ease tensions. According to a White House fact sheet, China committed to suspending all retaliatory tariffs that had been in place since March 4, 2025. This includes tariffs on a wide range of U.S. agricultural products such as corn, soybeans, wheat, cotton, pork, and beef. Additionally, China pledged to purchase at least 12 million metric tons of U.S. soybeans by the end of 2025. The agreement also addresses other key areas, with China agreeing to suspend export controls on rare earth minerals and take measures to stop the flow of fentanyl precursors to the United States. In return, the U.S. will lower certain tariffs on Chinese imports. While the White House detailed numerous specific commitments, some analysts note that the Chinese government's account of the deal is less detailed, suggesting the agreement should be seen as a temporary pause in an ongoing strategic conflict. <9> A government shutdown led to the suspension of USDA crop reporting services; including the monthly WASDE report; in the absence of these official benchmarks, traders would rely more on other market indicators <10> The Organic Farmers Association reported on proposed legislation aimed at preventing fraud in imported organic feedstuffs, including corn.; The bill would require the USDA's National Organic Program to conduct more rigorous residue testing on high-risk imported organic commodities.; The bill would require the USDA's National Organic Program to report the findings to Congress annually.
